# Your first FEM code: two springs in series {#sec-two-springs-code}

::: {.callout-note}
## Repository snapshot

**Course edition:** 2026--27\
**Target snapshot:** `2026-27/S01-two-springs`

This is the initial code snapshot. There is no preceding snapshot.
:::

## Purpose of the example

This chapter accompanies `two_springs.jl`, the first pure-Julia MiniFEM example,
which applies the direct stiffness method to the two-spring system shown in
@fig-carts-springs.

The mechanical formulation, hand assembly, and analytical solution were derived
in @sec-two-springs-theory. In this chapter, the mathematical objects and finite
element operations are mapped to their corresponding Julia representations.

The script is intentionally written as a top-level, dependency-free program.
Every finite element operation remains visible, and only the basic Julia
constructs introduced in @sec-julia-essentials are used. The implementation
favours explicit, [imperative logic](../glossary.qmd#gls-imperative-programming)
over compact syntax or custom abstractions, so that the program can be read in
the same order as the hand calculation.

## Learning objectives

After completing this chapter, you should be able to:

- relate the mathematical formulation of the two-spring problem to its Julia
  implementation;
- explain how element data, connectivity, and degrees of freedom are represented
  and used in the finite element procedure;
- follow the assembly, application of boundary conditions, and solution of the
  global system;
- verify the numerical results against independently derived reference values.

## Running the example

Run the example from the directory containing the file:

```bash
julia two_springs.jl
```

## Mathematical specification used by the script

The code implements the formulation derived in @sec-two-springs-theory. The
mathematical information required by the script is summarized below.

For every spring element,

$$
  \mathbf{K}^{(e)}=k_e
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & -1\\
  -1 & 1
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The mathematical matrix $\mathbf{K}^{(e)}$ is represented in the Julia code by
the variable `K_e`.

The assembled equilibrium equations can be written as

$$
  \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}
  =
  \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}+\mathbf{r},
$$

where $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}$ contains the known applied nodal forces and
$\mathbf{r}$ contains the unknown support reaction.

The prescribed displacement is imposed by modifying the assembled system. After
this modification, the system solved by the code is

$$
  \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}.
$$

Here, `K` and `f` denote the modified algebraic system used by the solver. The
original assembled stiffness matrix is preserved as `K_original`, so that
physical quantities such as the support reaction and strain energy can be later
recovered from the unmodified system.

For the present model,

$$
  k_1=1\ \mathrm{N/mm},
  \qquad
  k_2=2\ \mathrm{N/mm},
  \qquad
  F=10\ \mathrm{N},
  \qquad
  u_2=0.
$$

The finite element model, global node numbering, and element connectivity are
shown in @fig-spring-cart-fem-model. The physical nodes are ordered from left to
right as global nodes 2, 3, and 1. Element 1 connects nodes 2 and 3, while
element 2 connects nodes 3 and 1.

The global displacement vector follows numerical node order:

$$
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1 & u_2 & u_3
  \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}.
$$

The expected reference results are

$$
  \mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{reference}}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  15 & 0 & 10
  \end{bmatrix}^{\mathsf T}\ \mathrm{mm},
  \qquad
  U_{\mathrm{reference}}=75\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
$$

## From mathematical objects to Julia data

  | Mathematical object                                          | Julia representation                                                             |
  | :----------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | number of nodes                                              | `num_nodes`                                                                      |
  | degrees of freedom per node                                  | `dofs_per_node`                                                                  |
  | total number of degrees of freedom                           | `total_dofs`                                                                     |
  | element connectivity                                         | `element_connectivity`                                                           |
  | spring stiffnesses                                           | `element_stiffness`                                                              |
  | element stiffness matrix $\mathbf{K}^{(e)}$                  | `K_e`                                                                            |
  | local-to-global degree-of-freedom map                        | `dof_map`                                                                        |
  | global stiffness matrix $\mathbf{K}$                         | `K`                                                                              |
  | known applied nodal-force vector $\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}$ | `f` after applied-force assembly and before displacement-constraint modification |
  | modified solver right-hand side $\widetilde{\mathbf{f}}$     | `f` after displacement-constraint modification                                   |
  | applied nodal forces                                         | `applied_forces`                                                                 |
  | constrained degrees of freedom                               | `constrained_dofs`                                                               |
  | displacement solution                                        | `u`                                                                              |
  | unmodified assembled stiffness matrix                        | `K_original`                                                                     |

Nodal coordinates are not stored in this first implementation because the spring
stiffnesses are supplied directly and the coordinates are not required for the
numerical calculation. They remain useful for describing and plotting the
physical model and will be introduced when later element formulations require
geometric information.

## Pseudocode summary of the finite element procedure

The program follows three main stages: pre-processing, processing, and
post-processing. The processing stage is further divided into assembly,
application of the boundary conditions, and solution.

```pseudocode
1. Pre-processing: Input Data
   - Define the number of nodes and displacement degrees of freedom per node
   - Define the element connectivity
   - Define the stiffness of each spring element
   - Define the constrained degrees of freedom
   - Define the applied nodal forces
   - Compute the total number of degrees of freedom and elements
   - Initialize the global stiffness matrix K
   - Initialize the global force vector f

2. Processing

   2.1 Assembly: Build Global K
       - For each element:
         - Read the element stiffness k_e
         - Construct the element stiffness matrix K_e
         - Build the local-to-global degree-of-freedom map
         - Add the entries of K_e to the corresponding entries of K
       - Display the assembled global stiffness matrix K

   2.2 Boundary Conditions
       - Copy the assembled matrix K as K_original
       - Add the applied nodal forces to f
       - For each constrained degree of freedom:
         - Set the corresponding row and column of K to zero
         - Set the corresponding diagonal entry of K to one
         - Set the corresponding entry of f to zero

   2.3 Solver
       - Solve the modified linear system K u = f
       - Display the computed and analytical displacement vectors for comparison

3. Post-processing: Strain Energy
   - Compute the total internal strain energy from
     1/2 u^T K_original u
   - Compute the analytical strain energy
   - Compare the numerical and analytical energy values
```

## Walkthrough of the Julia script

The Julia language features used below were introduced in @sec-julia-essentials.
In this walkthrough we identify the finite element meaning of each data
structure and computational step.

### Model dimensions and input data

The model dimensions are

```julia
num_nodes = 3
dofs_per_node = 1
total_dofs = num_nodes * dofs_per_node
```

As there is one displacement degree of freedom per node, `total_dofs` is equal
to `3`.

The element connectivity is stored as a matrix:

```julia
element_connectivity = [
    2 3;
    3 1
]
```

Each row represents one element. The first and second columns contain the global
nodes associated with local nodes 1 and 2:

  | element number | global node corresponding to local node 1 | global node corresponding to local node 2 |
  | -------------: | ----------------------------------------: | ----------------------------------------: |
  |              1 |                                         2 |                                         3 |
  |              2 |                                         3 |                                         1 |

The spring stiffnesses are stored in the same element order:

```julia
element_stiffness = [1.0, 2.0]
```

meaning that `element_stiffness[1]` belongs to element 1 and
`element_stiffness[2]` belongs to element 2.

::: {.callout-important}
## Consistent units

The script stores physical quantities as ordinary numerical values; it does not
attach or check units. The input data must therefore use a consistent unit
system. In this example, forces are in newtons, lengths in millimeters, spring
stiffnesses in newtons per millimeter, and strain energy in newton millimeters.
:::

The number of elements is obtained from the number of rows in the connectivity
matrix:

```julia
num_elements = size(element_connectivity, 1)
```

The applied force and homogeneous displacement constraint are represented by

```julia
applied_force = 10.0
applied_forces = [(1, applied_force)]
constrained_dofs = [2]
```

Each entry of `applied_forces` associates a global degree-of-freedom index with
a force value. Here, the force acts at global degree of freedom 1.

The vector `constrained_dofs` contains the index of the constrained degree of
freedom. Because the prescribed displacement is zero in this first snapshot,
there is no need for a data structure analogous to `applied_forces`; the code
therefore stores only the constrained degree-of-freedom index.

::: {.callout-important}
## Numerical order is not geometric order

The physical nodes are arranged from left to right as `2 -> 3 -> 1`, whereas the
global arrays follow numerical order. Consequently,

```text
u[1] = displacement of the rightmost node
u[2] = displacement of the fixed left node
u[3] = displacement of the internal node
```
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Array indices and model identifiers

In this script, global degree-of-freedom numbers are used directly as Julia
array indices. The internal degree-of-freedom numbering must therefore form the
consecutive sequence

```text
1, 2, ..., total_dofs
```

External mesh or data-file labels do not need to follow this rule. Arbitrary
labels such as `3, 4, 5, 99` can be retained, provided that they are mapped to
consecutive internal indices such as `1, 2, 3, 4` before the algebraic arrays
are constructed.
:::

### Global arrays

The global stiffness matrix and force vector are initialized as zero-filled
arrays:

```julia
K = zeros(total_dofs, total_dofs)
f = zeros(total_dofs)
```

For this problem, `K` is a `3 x 3` matrix and `f` is a vector with three
entries. They begin at zero because element stiffness contributions and applied
nodal forces will be accumulated into them.

### Element loop

The assembly stage visits each spring element in turn. The computational part of
the element loop is

```julia
for e in 1:num_elements
    k_e = element_stiffness[e]
    K_e = [
        +k_e -k_e;
        -k_e +k_e
    ]

    dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]

    for i in 1:2
        I = dof_map[i]
        for j in 1:2
            J = dof_map[j]
            K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
        end
    end
end
```

For each element, the script retrieves its stiffness, constructs its element
stiffness matrix, builds the local-to-global degree-of-freedom map, and adds the
element contribution to the global stiffness matrix. One iteration of this loop
therefore performs the element-level operations required by the direct stiffness
procedure.

### Constructing the element matrix

For the current element, the stiffness value is retrieved with

```julia
k_e = element_stiffness[e]
```

and the mathematical element matrix

$$
  \mathbf{K}^{(e)}=k_e
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1 & -1\\
  -1 & 1
  \end{bmatrix}
$$

is represented by

```julia
K_e = [
    +k_e -k_e;
    -k_e +k_e
]
```

`K_e` contains the stiffness matrix of the current element and must not be
confused with the assembled global matrix `K`.

### Building the local-to-global map

For element `e`, the global degrees of freedom are read from the connectivity
matrix:

```julia
dof_map = [element_connectivity[e, 1], element_connectivity[e, 2]]
```

The resulting maps are

```text
element 1: dof_map = [2, 3]
element 2: dof_map = [3, 1]
```

Because the model has one degree of freedom per node, the connected node numbers
are also the global degree-of-freedom numbers. This equivalence will no longer
hold automatically when several degrees of freedom are attached to each node.

The two entries of `dof_map` correspond, in order, to local degrees of freedom 1
and 2. The map therefore identifies the global rows and columns into which the
entries of `K_e` are assembled.

### Assembling the global stiffness matrix

The element matrix must be transferred from its local ordering to the global
matrix ordering. Suppose that the local degrees of freedom $\{1,2\}$ correspond
to the global degrees of freedom $\{2,3\}$:

```text
local degree of freedom:   1   2
global degree of freedom:  2   3
```

This correspondence defines a local-to-global map

$$
  g(1)=2,
  \qquad
  g(2)=3.
$$

An entry of the element matrix is identified by a local row index and a local
column index. For a two-degree-of-freedom element, all element entries are
therefore represented by the Cartesian product

$$
  \{1,2\}\times\{1,2\}
  =
  \{(1,1),\ (1,2),\ (2,1),\ (2,2)\}.
$$

The local-to-global map is applied separately to the row and column indices:

$$
  (i,j)
  \longmapsto
  \bigl(g(i),g(j)\bigr).
$$

For element 1,

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  (1,1)&\longmapsto(2,2),\\
  (1,2)&\longmapsto(2,3),\\
  (2,1)&\longmapsto(3,2),\\
  (2,2)&\longmapsto(3,3).
  \end{aligned}
$$

Consequently,

$$
  \begin{aligned}
  K_{22} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{11},\\
  K_{23} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{12},\\
  K_{32} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{21},\\
  K_{33} &\mathrel{+}= K^{(1)}_{22}.
  \end{aligned}
$$

The nested loops implement exactly this operation:

```julia
for i in 1:2
    I = dof_map[i]
    for j in 1:2
        J = dof_map[j]
        K[I, J] += K_e[i, j]
    end
end
```

Lowercase `i` and `j` identify local row and column positions, whereas uppercase
`I` and `J` identify the corresponding global positions. In mathematical form,
the operation performed for every local pair is

$$
  K_{g(i),g(j)}\mathrel{+}=K^{(e)}_{ij}.
$$

The contribution is added rather than overwritten because different elements may
contribute to the same global matrix entry. In this model, both elements
contribute to `K[3, 3]`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise -- Modify one element stiffness

Change the stiffness of element 2 from

```julia
element_stiffness = [1.0, 2.0]
```

to

```julia
element_stiffness = [1.0, 3.0]
```

Before running the script, predict which entries of the assembled global
stiffness matrix `K` will change and which will remain unchanged.

Then run the script and compare the new matrix with the original one. Use the
connectivity of element 2 and its local-to-global degree-of-freedom map to
explain the result.

For this exercise, focus only on the assembled matrix `K`; the hard-coded
analytical displacement later in the script corresponds to the original
stiffness values.
:::

### Preserving the assembled matrix

Before the displacement condition modifies the global matrix, the script
preserves the assembled physical stiffness matrix:

```julia
K_original = copy(K)
```

This distinction is important mechanically. `K_original` represents the
assembled stiffness matrix before the displacement constraint is imposed,
whereas `K` will subsequently be modified into the algebraic system matrix used
by the solver. The original matrix is required for the strain-energy computation
and can also be used to recover reactions.

The Julia semantics of `copy` were introduced in @sec-julia-essentials; here its
purpose is to keep the original physical operator available after `K` is
modified.

### Assembling the applied force

The applied nodal-force data are transferred into the global vector with

```julia
for (dof, value) in applied_forces
    f[dof] += value
end
```

For the current data, the resulting vector is

$$
  \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  10\\0\\0
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{N}.
$$

The support reaction is not entered as an applied load because it is unknown. It
can be recovered after the displacement solution from the original equilibrium
equations.

### Imposing the homogeneous displacement constraint

The zero displacement at degree of freedom 2 is imposed with

```julia
for dof in constrained_dofs
    for i in 1:total_dofs
        K[i, dof] = 0.0
        K[dof, i] = 0.0
    end

    K[dof, dof] = 1.0
    f[dof] = 0.0
end
```

For each constrained degree of freedom, the code zeros the corresponding row and
column, places one on the diagonal, and sets the corresponding right-hand side
entry to zero. For the present problem, the modified system is

$$
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2 & 0 & -2\\
  0 & 1 & 0\\
  -2 & 0 & 3
  \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix}
  u_1\\u_2\\u_3
  \end{bmatrix}
  =
  \begin{bmatrix}
  10\\0\\0
  \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Its second equation is exactly $u_2=0$.

In @sec-two-springs-theory, the modified arrays were denoted by
$\widetilde{\mathbf{K}}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf{f}}$. The script does not
introduce new variable names for them: `K` and `f` are [modified in
place](../glossary.qmd#gls-modified-in-place). After this operation, `K`
represents the modified algebraic system matrix rather than the original
physical stiffness matrix. The original assembled matrix remains available as
`K_original`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scope of this implementation

This row-and-column modification is sufficient for a homogeneous prescribed
displacement. A nonzero prescribed value also requires a consistent correction
of the right-hand side and is introduced in a later snapshot.
:::

### Solving the linear system

The modified system is solved with

```julia
u = K \ f
```

which computes the solution of

$$
  \mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}.
$$

The backslash operator was introduced in @sec-julia-essentials. Its finite
element role here is simply to solve the constrained global equilibrium system
for the unknown nodal displacements.

### Comparing displacement results

The reference displacement vector is stored in global order:

```julia
u_analytical = [15.0, 0.0, 10.0]
```

and is displayed alongside the numerical solution for comparison.

### Computing the internal strain energy

The numerical internal strain energy is computed with the original assembled
matrix:

```julia
strain_energy_global = 0.5 * transpose(u) * K_original * u
```

This is the Julia representation of

$$
  U=\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{u}^{\mathsf T}
  \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{original}}\mathbf{u}.
$$

The independent reference value is computed from the two spring stiffnesses:

```julia
k_1 = element_stiffness[1]
k_2 = element_stiffness[2]
strain_energy_analytical = 0.5 * applied_force^2 * (1 / k_1 + 1 / k_2)
```

The derivation of this expression is given in @sec-two-springs-theory. The
important point here is that the numerical energy uses the original assembled
stiffness matrix, not the matrix after the displacement constraint has been
inserted.

## Verification

A program result should not be accepted merely because the script runs. The
present example provides several checks against quantities already derived
independently.

### Assembled stiffness matrix

Before boundary conditions, the expected global matrix is

$$
  \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{expected}}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  2 & 0 & -2\\
  0 & 1 & -1\\
  -2 & -1 & 3
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{N/mm}.
$$

The matrix should be symmetric, and each row should sum to zero before
displacement constraints are imposed, reflecting the rigid-translation mode of
the unconstrained assembly.

### Displacements

The numerical solution should be

$$
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  15\\0\\10
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm}.
$$

Remember that the entries are in global numerical order. The rightmost node is
the first entry, the fixed left node is the second, and the internal node is the
third.

### Element elongations and spring forces

Using the element connectivity,

$$
  \delta_1=u_3-u_2=10\ \mathrm{mm},
  \qquad
  \delta_2=u_1-u_3=5\ \mathrm{mm}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
  F_s^{(1)}=k_1\delta_1=10\ \mathrm{N},
  \qquad
  F_s^{(2)}=k_2\delta_2=10\ \mathrm{N}.
$$

The equal internal spring forces confirm equilibrium at the internal node.

### Internal strain energy

Both the global quadratic form and the independent spring expression should give

$$
  U=75\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
$$

The script reports the absolute difference between the numerical and analytical
energy values. For this small problem, the difference should be zero or a very
small value arising from floating-point rounding. Approximate comparisons and
numerical tolerances are discussed in Part II of @sec-julia-essentials.

Recovery of the support reaction provides one further equilibrium check and is
left as Exercise 3.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 1 -- Change the applied force

Keep $k_1=1\ \mathrm{N/mm}$ and $k_2=2\ \mathrm{N/mm}$, but set

$$
  F=6\ \mathrm{N}.
$$

Before running the script:

1. compute the global displacement vector;
2. compute the internal strain energy;
3. predict how displacements and energy scale relative to the original problem.

Then update `applied_force` and `u_analytical` and run the script. The expected
results are

$$
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  9\\0\\6
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm},
  \qquad
  U=27\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 2 -- Change both spring stiffnesses

Use

$$
  k_1=2\ \mathrm{N/mm},
  \qquad
  k_2=4\ \mathrm{N/mm},
  \qquad
  F=8\ \mathrm{N}.
$$

Update `element_stiffness`, `applied_force`, and `u_analytical`. Determine the
reference displacement vector and strain energy before running the code. The
expected results are

$$
  \mathbf{u}=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  6\\0\\4
  \end{bmatrix}
  \ \mathrm{mm},
  \qquad
  U=24\ \mathrm{N\,mm}.
$$
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Exercise 3 -- Recover the support reaction

The reaction can be recovered from the original assembled equilibrium equations,

$$
  \mathbf{r}
  =
  \mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{original}}\mathbf{u}
  -
  \mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}.
$$

After solving for `u`, reconstruct the applied-load vector
$\mathbf{f}_{\mathrm{app}}$ for the present problem and implement this relation
in Julia.

Check that only the constrained degree of freedom has a nonzero reaction and
that the applied force and support reaction satisfy global equilibrium.
:::

## What comes next

This first snapshot exposes the core direct stiffness calculation in a single
script. Later snapshots will progressively separate recurring operations from
problem-specific data and make the implementation easier to reuse and verify.
